intro.standard: Find your way around the solar system and see what each world is like.
intro.simple: Fly to planets and moons and take a close look.

intro.standard: Speed time up, run it backwards or jump to any date.
intro.simple: Make time go fast, go backwards or jump to another day.

intro.standard: How big the worlds really are, and how far apart.
intro.simple: How big is everything, and how far away?

intro.standard: Sunlight makes day, night and eclipses, and even light needs time to travel.
intro.simple: The Sun makes day and night. And light needs time to get anywhere.

intro.standard: Put worlds next to each other at their true sizes.
intro.simple: Put two worlds next to each other and see which is bigger.

teachers.title: For teachers
teachers.intro: Show the solar system to a class: projector, keyboard, links and QR codes.

intro.standard: Hunt for worlds, find your age on Mars and take a picture to keep.
intro.simple: Play a hunt, find out how old you are on Mars, and take a picture.

intro.standard: Orbitalia is free and open source: it gets better with every bug you report and every idea you send.
intro.simple: Tell us when something is broken, or when you have an idea.

what.standard: About a minute that starts close on Earth at its real size and pulls back until Earth is smaller than a pixel, then draws everything bigger so you can see it. Every caption stays up long enough to read it aloud.
what.simple: A film that flies from Earth out to the whole solar system. It goes slowly, so you can read every word.

why.standard: It makes the point of the app before anyone reads a word: space is huge and almost empty. It works without sound.
why.simple: It shows how big and how empty space is.

standard: It plays once, on the first visit; “Skip intro”, a drag or Esc ends it at any time.
To stay on a caption, press Space, tap the scene or press the pause button; do it again to carry on. While it is paused you can turn the view without ending it.
“Next” (or the right arrow key) goes straight on to the next part; while paused, one part at a time.
After the first opening the app asks once whether you want a quick look at what you can do (see “A quick look”).
To see it again, open the arrow next to Help and choose “Play the opening again”.
“Show how to move around” in the same menu brings back the hints for dragging, zooming and clicking.
simple: It plays the first time you come.
Press Space or tap the picture to stop it. Do it again to go on.
“Next” shows the next part.
To watch it again, press the arrow next to Help, then “Play the opening again”.

what.standard: A one-minute tour of the best features, shown working in the scene: flying to a planet, true scale, travelling in time, comparing worlds and watching light crawl, then a step for teachers on presentation mode and the way to this page.
what.simple: A one-minute trip through the best things the app can do.

why.standard: Most people never find these on their own. One minute shows what the app can do, and each step points at the button that does it.
why.simple: You see the coolest things right away, and where the buttons for them are.

standard: On your first visit, after the opening, answer “Yes, show me”. It is asked only once in this browser, and never over a shared link or while presenting.
It moves on by itself; Back, Next and the arrow keys step it, and “Skip the rest” or × leave it at any time, back to a calm view.
To see it again, open the arrow next to Help and choose “Take the quick look again”.
simple: After the opening, press “Yes, show me”.
Watch, or press Next.
To see it again, press the arrow next to Help.

what.standard: Click a planet, a moon or its name and the camera flies there: it pulls back, crosses the gap and comes down close.
what.simple: Click a planet and you fly there.

why.standard: The flight shows how far apart the worlds are, and a readout says how long light, a spacecraft and a car would need for the same trip.
why.simple: On the way you see how far it is, and how long a car would need. Years and years!

standard: Point at a planet or its name: a ring appears with “Click to fly there”.
Click or tap it. To land at once, press Skip in the readout.
On a small dot, click anywhere near it: the target is generous.
The house button at the top left (or Esc) is the way back to the whole solar system; a click on empty space leaves the view where it is.
simple: Move the mouse over a planet. A ring shows up.
Click it. Now watch the trip.
Press “Be there now” if you do not want to wait.
Press the house button at the top left to see all the planets again.

title.simple: Find a world by its name

what.standard: The box at the top left lists the Sun, every planet and the moons with a story; type to search.
what.simple: Type the name of a planet or moon, and you go there.

why.standard: Some worlds are too small to click, and a class can follow along when you name where you are going.
why.simple: Some moons are too tiny to click. The name box finds them.

standard: Click the box at the top left and type a name, such as “Titan”.
Pick it from the list: the camera flies there.
Press ← or → to visit the next world of the same family; the house button or Esc takes you back to the whole system.
simple: Click the box at the top left.
Type a name, like Titan, and pick it.
Press Esc to see the whole solar system again.

title.standard: Turn, zoom and move the view

what.standard: Drag to turn around the world you are looking at, zoom in and out, and slide the view anywhere, even into empty space between the planets.
what.simple: Turn the view, zoom in and out, and move to any place, even empty space.

why.standard: Looking from the side, from above and from far away is how the shapes of orbits and the emptiness of space become real.
why.simple: From far away you see how empty space is.

standard: Turn: drag with the left mouse button or one finger.
Zoom: the mouse wheel, a trackpad pinch, or two fingers.
Move sideways: drag with the right button, Shift + drag, or two fingers together. Let go on a planet and the view centres on it.
In empty space a badge shows where you are; “Centre on …” or “Back to overview” brings you home.
simple: Drag to turn the view.
Use the mouse wheel or two fingers to zoom.
Drag with the right mouse button to slide the view away.

what.standard: The screen belongs to space. Only what you are looking at, the way back and the time stay on it; everything else waits behind four buttons at the bottom right: Tours, Layers, Scale and Tools. While you turn, zoom or fly, the controls step back a little.
what.simple: Most buttons stay out of the way so you can see space. Four buttons at the bottom right open the rest.

why.standard: The planets are the lesson, not the buttons: the class sees the solar system, and every control is still at most two clicks away.
why.simple: You see more of space, and every button is still close by.

standard: Top left: the house button (back to the whole system), the name of the world in view and its card; the arrow on the card opens its facts, moons and stories.
Bottom: play, pause and the date; the button with the speed (like 1x) opens Now, the speeds and the spin.

Bottom right: Tours, Layers (what is drawn), Scale (how big and how far) and Tools (the speed of light, tonight's sky, spacecraft, your birthday, the scavenger hunt, side by side, walking the solar system, the picture dictionary and taking a picture). One panel opens at a time; × closes it.
Top right: Present, Share, the crossed-out eye that hides everything (H brings it back), sound, Help and the language.
simple: The house button at the top left takes you back to all the planets.
Press Layers, Scale or Tools at the bottom right to find more.
Press the crossed-out eye at the top right to hide all the buttons. Press H to get them back.

what.standard: When you look at a world, a card shows its name and facts you can picture: its size in Earths, how long sunlight takes to get there, how long its year is and what you would weigh there.
what.simple: A card tells you about the world you are looking at: how big it is, how far from the Sun, and what you would weigh there.

why.standard: Comparisons stick where big numbers do not; the exact number is always right underneath.
why.simple: “Nine Earths wide” is easier to picture than a big number.

standard: Fly to a world: its card appears with its name and one sentence.
Press the arrow on the card to open its facts, moons and stories; it stays open for the next world.
“Read more in the dictionary” opens its page, “Compare with…” puts it next to another world.
Under the comparison, “Shrink the Sun to a basketball…” finds the world on the walk across the school field.
The last line of the open card says where the picture of the world comes from: a spacecraft’s map, or painted after spacecraft photos where no complete map exists.
simple: Fly to a planet.
Read its card.
Press the little arrow to see more.

what.standard: Every planet’s natural moons, from our Moon to the tiny rocks around Saturn; the moons with a story are shown first.
what.simple: Planets have moons. Jupiter and Saturn have lots of them!

why.standard: A moon system is a small solar system: Io’s volcanoes, Europa’s hidden ocean and Titan’s thick air all happen around a planet.
why.simple: Some moons have volcanoes, and some have oceans under the ice.

standard: Fly to a planet and open its card with the arrow: it lists its best-known moons. Click one to fly there.
“See the whole moon system” steps back until every orbit fits.
“Show … smaller moons” or the All moons switch (under Layers) adds the many small ones; a moon’s card has “Read its story”.
A moon’s card says where its surface comes from: a spacecraft’s map, filled in where no one has ever looked, or painted from what is known.
simple: Fly to Jupiter.
Open its card with the little arrow and click a moon to fly to it.
Press “See all its moons”.

what.standard: Switches decide what is drawn: orbits, names, moons, all moons, dot markers, the names of the orbits and “Always lit”.
what.simple: Switches turn the names, the paths and the dots on and off.

why.standard: Hide the names for a quiz, or switch the markers off at true scale to see how invisible the planets really are.
why.simple: Hide the names and ask your friends which planet is which!

standard: Press Layers at the bottom right: the switches open above it.
Press L to hide or show every name at once.
All moons works only while Moons is on.
Rest the pointer on a switch, or press and hold it, to read what it does; a greyed-out switch says what to turn on first.
simple: Press Layers at the bottom right.
Click a switch to turn it off, and again to turn it back on.
Press L to hide all the names.
Hold the mouse over a switch to find out what it does.

what.standard: Every switch, choice and button in the solar system explains itself in one sentence: what it does and why you would use it. A greyed-out switch says what to turn on first.
what.simple: Every switch and button can tell you what it does.

why.standard: You can plan a lesson without flipping every switch to find out what it does: what the markers are, or why “Always lit” hides day and night.
why.simple: You never have to guess what a switch does.

standard: Mouse: rest the pointer on a switch, or on its name, for half a second.
Keyboard: move to it with Tab; screen readers read the same sentence.
Touch: press and hold the switch or its name. A quick tap still just switches it.
Esc closes the hint.
simple: Hold the mouse still over a switch.
On a tablet, press and hold the switch with your finger.

what.standard: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune have rings, drawn at their real sizes, tilted with their planet and casting real shadows.
what.simple: Four planets have rings: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

why.standard: Saturn’s rings open and close over the years as it goes round the Sun, and Uranus’s stand on end because the planet lies on its side.
why.simple: Saturn’s rings are very thin. From the side they almost disappear!

standard: Fly to Saturn and drag down until you look at the rings edge-on.
Travel a few years in time to see them tip towards the Sun and away.
Visit Uranus and Neptune for thin, dark rings.
simple: Fly to Saturn.
Drag to look at the rings from the side.
Then fly to Uranus. Its rings stand up!

what.standard: Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake are real worlds in the app, with their moons, from Charon to Dysnomia.
what.simple: Pluto and four other small round worlds, with their moons.

why.standard: Pluto’s card tells why it stopped being a planet in 2006: we learned more, Pluto did not change. That is how science works.
why.simple: You can find out why Pluto is not a planet any more.

standard: Type “Pluto” in the box at the top left and pick it: it is shown even while Small bodies is off.
Open the card with its arrow: Charon is listed there; “See the whole moon system” frames all five moons.
← / → move to the next dwarf planet.
simple: Type “Pluto” in the box at the top left.
Pick Pluto and you fly there.

what.standard: Five comets on their real, stretched orbits grow a glowing head and two tails as they near the Sun, and lose them as they leave.
what.simple: Comets grow a long tail when they come close to the Sun.

why.standard: The tail always points away from the Sun, so a comet that is leaving flies tail first: something to see, not only to be told.
why.simple: The tail always points away from the Sun, even when the comet flies away!

standard: Pick Halley or Encke in the box at the top left (group Comets).
Open its card with the arrow and press “Watch it pass the Sun”: the app goes to its next visit and plays it in about a minute and a half.
Watch which way the tail points on the way in and on the way out.
simple: Pick Halley in the box at the top left.
Open its card with the little arrow and press “Watch it fly past the Sun”.

what.standard: Every world turns on its tilted axis at its true speed: Venus backwards, Uranus on its side, and the Moon always showing us the same face.
what.simple: Every planet spins around. One turn is one day there.

why.standard: Spin makes day and night, and the tilt makes the seasons; the spin setting slows the turning so you can watch days pass while time runs fast.
why.simple: Spinning makes day and night. Venus even spins the other way!

standard: Fly to Earth and make time run faster.
Press the speed button in the time bar and, under Spin, choose Slowed or Slow motion to watch the days, Stopped to hold it still.
Realistic puts every world back to its true position for the date.
simple: Fly to Earth.
Make time go faster.
Press the speed button at the bottom and choose Slow motion to watch Earth spin.

what.standard: Hold Earth still and watch everything else move around it, the way the sky moves for us: Mars loops backwards, the Moon goes through its phases.
what.simple: Keep Earth still and watch how the other planets move from here.

why.standard: For two thousand years people explained these loops with Earth at the centre; seeing both views side by side shows why the Sun-centred one won.
why.simple: From Earth, Mars sometimes seems to walk backwards. Now you can see why.

standard: Click “Sun-centred” next to the name box and choose “Seen from Earth: the planets” or “Seen from Earth: the Moon”.
Watch the badge at the top: it says what the selected world is doing in our sky.
“Hold … still” works for any world; “Back to Sun-centred” returns.
simple: Click “Sun in the middle” at the top left.
Choose “From Earth: the planets”.
Watch Mars make a loop.

title.standard: What is in the sky tonight

what.standard: Which planets and what Moon you can see tonight from your town: when, in which direction, how high, and whether you need binoculars.
what.simple: Find out which planets you can see from your town tonight, and where to look.

why.standard: It is the bridge from the screen to the real sky, and “Why can I see it?” shows the Earth, Sun and planet lined up in 3D.
why.simple: Go outside and find Jupiter or Venus with your own eyes!

standard: Open Tools at the bottom right, choose “Tonight’s sky” and pick your town (the app never asks for your location on its own).
Read the list: what you can see, when, where and with what.
Press “Why can I see it?” next to a planet to see the reason in space.
simple: Press Tools, then “Tonight’s sky”.
Pick your town. Ask a grown-up before using the device’s location.
Read where to look, then go outside!

what.standard: Voyager, Pioneer, New Horizons, Cassini, Juno, Parker, JWST and Europa Clipper, drawn where they really are on the date on screen, with their paths and milestones.
what.simple: Real space probes that people built, shown where they are right now.

why.standard: Voyager 1 is still sending messages from far beyond the planets: its card shows how long its signal takes to reach us, and why the trip took so many gravity assists.
why.simple: Voyager 1 left Earth when your grandparents were young, and it is still flying. A message from it takes almost a day to reach us!

standard: Open Tools at the bottom right, choose “Real spacecraft” and pick a craft: the view flies to it.
Its card shows launch, distance, signal time and milestones; a milestone takes time to that moment.
“Show every path” draws all their routes at once; the Spacecraft switch hides them.
simple: Press Tools at the bottom right.
Choose “Real spacecraft”, then Voyager 1.
Read how far away it is.

what.standard: A page for the Sun and each planet, with a big turning globe, its surface maps and the key numbers explained.
what.simple: A page for the Sun and every planet, with a big spinning picture.

why.standard: It is the quiet way to read about one world at a time, and to peel off its clouds or see its mountains and oceans.
why.simple: Read about one planet at a time, and see its mountains and clouds.

standard: Open Tools at the bottom right and choose “Picture dictionary”: it opens on the world you are looking at. Or press “Read more in the dictionary” on a world’s card.
Pick a world in the row of dots at the top, then Surface, Terrain, Oceans or Clouds where it has them.
simple: Press Tools, then “Planet book”.
Pick a planet in the row of dots at the top.
Try Terrain and Clouds to change the picture.

title.standard: Sound and the sounds of space

what.standard: Optional sound: a background hum that changes with where you are, soft tones when you fly and arrive, and real recordings made by spacecraft at the Sun, Earth, Jupiter and Saturn.
what.simple: Turn on sound to hear a hum, a whoosh when you fly, and real recordings from space probes.

why.standard: Space itself is silent; the recordings are radio and plasma waves measured by antennas and turned into sound, which is a surprise worth hearing. Everything also works with sound off.
why.simple: Space has no air, so it is silent. But space probes measured invisible waves, and we can listen to them!

standard: Sound is always off when the app opens. Press the speaker button at the top right, or M, to turn it on.
The arrow next to it opens the volume, the background hum, the motion sounds and “Listen to space”.
Fly to the Sun, Earth, Jupiter or Saturn and play its recording from the card; the text says what you hear.
simple: Press the speaker button at the top right.
Fly to Jupiter.
Press play on its card and listen.

what.standard: Orbitalia speaks English, German, Czech, Spanish and French, each at three reading levels: simple, standard and advanced.
what.simple: Read everything in your language, and in easy words.

why.standard: The same view can be explained to a nine-year-old and to a sixth-former, and a shared link keeps both choices.
why.simple: Simple words for younger readers, more detail for older ones.

standard: Open the language menu at the top right (it shows EN, DE, …).
Pick a language and a reading level; every page and link follows.
simple: Click the button with EN at the top right.
Choose your language, and choose Simple.

what.standard: Buttons at the bottom run time forwards or backwards, pause it, and pick a speed from real time to ten years a second.
what.simple: Buttons at the bottom make time go, stop, go faster or go backwards.

why.standard: At real time nothing seems to move; at a month a second the inner planets race and the outer ones crawl, which is Kepler’s law you can see.
why.simple: Speed time up and see that planets near the Sun go round much faster.

standard: Press ▶ to play, ⏸ to pause, ◀ to run backwards (Space pauses too).
The button next to the date shows the speed (like 1x): press it and pick another, or press + and −.
“Now”, in the same place, brings you back to the present.
simple: Press the play button at the bottom.
Press the speed button next to the date and pick 1 month/s.
Press Space to stop.

what.standard: Click the date to jump to any day from the year 1000 to 2999, or to a famous moment such as the Moon landing or Mars at its closest.
what.simple: Go to any day, like the day of the Moon landing.

why.standard: Real events happened where the planets really were; the scene shows the sky on that date, and time stops when you arrive.
why.simple: You can see where the planets were on a special day.

standard: Click the date and time at the bottom.
Choose “Pick a date” and click the year, the month and the day (famous moments are under “Sky events”).
The planets glide there and time stops; press play to run on.
simple: Click the date at the bottom.
Pick “Mars at its closest” or pick a day.
Watch the planets move there.

title.standard: Sky events: eclipses, transits and alignments

what.standard: A list of eclipses, transits of Venus and Mercury, planets gathering in the sky, close approaches of Mars, moons' shadows and Saturn's rings edge-on, past and coming up. Choosing one sets everything: the date, true scale and a view from space, with a switch to the view from Earth through a telescope.
what.simple: Pick an eclipse or another sky show, and the app takes you there: the right day, the right place to look from.

why.standard: Each event is a geometry lesson in one picture: why the Moon covers the Sun exactly, why eclipses do not happen every month, what "the planets align" really means. Switching between the view from space and the view from Earth is the lesson.
why.simple: You see why an eclipse happens: from space, and from the Earth where people watched it.

standard: Click the date at the bottom and choose “Sky events”.
Pick an event, for example “Total solar eclipse” (8 April 2024).
Switch between “From space” and “From Earth” on the card; press “Leave” to go back to where you were.
simple: Click the date at the bottom, then “Sky events”.
Pick an eclipse.
Press “From Earth” to see the Moon cover the Sun.

what.standard: At very high speeds a warning names the world that moves too fast to follow and how many laps it makes each second.
what.simple: When time goes super fast, a note tells you which planet is going too fast to see.

why.standard: Like a wagon wheel in a film, a planet that laps more than a sixth of its orbit per picture can seem to stand still or go backwards; the note explains what you really see.
why.simple: A very fast planet can look like it stops or goes backwards. It does not really!

standard: Press the speed button next to the date and pick the fastest speed, 10 years/s.
Read the line under the time bar; choose a slower speed or pause and it goes away.
simple: Press the speed button and pick the fastest speed.
Read the note, then pick a slower speed.

title.standard: True scale and the scale presets

what.standard: The scene normally draws the worlds bigger and closer together so you can see them; one click shows real sizes and real distances.
what.simple: Normally the planets are drawn much too big. One click shows how small they really are.

why.standard: At true scale the planets vanish into empty space: the most surprising lesson in the app, and a statement always says how far the picture is from the truth.
why.simple: At real size you cannot even see the planets. Space is very, very empty!

standard: Press Scale at the bottom right (it names the scale on screen) and click True scale, Textbook or Everything visible, or press S.
The Sizes and Distances switches change one lie at a time.
At true scale, the dots show where the planets are; turn Markers off (under Layers) to see how little is left.
simple: Press Scale at the bottom right.
Click True scale.
Where did the planets go? The dots show where they are.

what.standard: Every flight between two worlds shows their true distance on the date on screen, and how long light, the fastest spacecraft and a car would take.
what.simple: When you fly to a planet, you see how far away it is.

why.standard: A car would need hundreds of years to reach Jupiter: the numbers turn a flight of a few seconds into a sense of real distance.
why.simple: A car would need hundreds of years to drive to Jupiter!

standard: Fly from one world to another.
Read the readout above the time controls while you travel; close it when you arrive.
The distance changes with the date, because the planets move.
simple: Fly from Earth to another planet.
Read the box above the time buttons.

title.standard: The asteroid belt is almost empty

what.standard: The Small bodies switch shows the asteroid belt and the Kuiper belt as fields of dots, plus the dwarf planets, seven named asteroids and five comets.
what.simple: A switch shows the asteroid belt, a ring of space rocks between Mars and Jupiter. It also shows the icy worlds beyond Neptune, and comets.

why.standard: Films show a crowded field of rocks. The card says the truth: each dot stands for about 380 asteroids, and neighbours are about a million km apart, so spacecraft fly straight through.
why.simple: In films it is full of rocks. In real space the rocks are very, very far apart.

standard: Press Layers at the bottom right and switch on “Small bodies”.
Read the note in the card at the top left.
Choose True scale in the Scale panel, then fly to Vesta or Ceres: the belt stays a sparse scatter.
simple: Press Layers and switch on “Small bodies”.
Read what the card says about the dots.

title.standard: Shrink the Sun and walk the solar system

what.standard: If the Sun were a basketball, Earth would be a pinhead 26 metres away: a page that turns the true scale into a walk across the school field.
what.simple: Make the Sun as big as a ball, and see how far you must walk to each planet.

why.standard: Walking the distances is the one scale lesson a class never forgets, and the table prints on one page.
why.simple: You can really walk it at school! Neptune is very far away.

standard: Open Tools at the bottom right and choose “Walk the solar system”, or press Scale and then “Shrink the Sun to a basketball…” at the bottom of its panel, in every scale.
On a world’s card, unfold the facts: under its comparison, “Shrink the Sun to a basketball and walk out to this world” opens the walk on that world.
Choose what the Sun is (an orange, a football, a basketball, an exercise ball) and a landmark to measure against.
Switch to Table and Print it to take outside.
simple: Press Tools, then “Walk the solar system”.
Or press Scale, then “Make the Sun a basketball…”.
Choose a ball for the Sun.
Read how far to walk to each planet.
Print the table and walk it outside.

what.standard: The Sun is the only light: every world has a day side and a night side, with Earth’s city lights in the dark.
what.simple: The Sun lights up one side of every planet. The other side is night.

why.standard: Seasons, phases and the midnight sun follow from the light alone: look at the Arctic in June.
why.simple: You can see where it is day and where it is night on Earth right now.

standard: Fly to Earth and turn the camera towards the line between day and night.
Travel to 21 June and 21 December to compare the poles.
The Always lit switch (under Layers) lights everything from where you look, to study the surfaces.
simple: Fly to Earth.
Turn the view to see the night side and its city lights.
Turn on Always lit under Layers to see every side.

what.standard: Shadows are real: the Moon’s shadow crosses Earth in a solar eclipse, and the Moon darkens inside Earth’s shadow in a lunar one, on the real dates.
what.simple: Sometimes the Moon hides the Sun, or goes into Earth’s shadow.

why.standard: Eclipses only happen when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up exactly; watching one from the side shows why they are rare.
why.simple: The Sun, Earth and Moon must be in a perfect line. That is why eclipses are rare.

standard: Open the link: the Moon inside Earth’s shadow on 14 March 2025.
Travel to 8 April 2024, fly to Earth and turn to its day side to find the Moon’s small, dark shadow.
Keep Always lit off, or the shadows disappear.
simple: Open the link and look at the dark Moon.
Drag to see Earth and the Sun behind it.

what.standard: Send a flash from the Sun or any planet and watch it spread at the real speed of light, ticking off each world as it arrives.
what.simple: Send a flash of light from the Sun and watch it travel to the planets.

why.standard: Light is the fastest thing there is, yet it needs 8 minutes to reach Earth and over 4 hours to reach Neptune: the size of the solar system in time.
why.simple: Light is super fast, but it still needs 8 minutes to get from the Sun to us!

standard: Open Tools at the bottom right, choose “Speed of light”, then “Send a flash”.
Pick where it starts; the list shows when it reaches each world.
Time switches to real time; a faster speed is allowed and the panel still counts true travel time.
To stop it, press “Stop the flash”, the × on its label or the × beside its clock under the name box, or X. Once it has passed Neptune it fades by itself.
simple: Press Tools, then “How fast is light?”.
Press “Send a flash”.
Watch the circle grow and reach the planets.
Press “Turn the light off” to stop it.

what.standard: How long a message from Earth takes to reach any world right now, there and back, and how that changes as the planets move.
what.simple: A message to Mars takes minutes to arrive. See how long for each world.

why.standard: Nobody can steer a Mars rover with a joystick: by the time it hears you, many minutes have passed.
why.simple: That is why you cannot drive a Mars robot like a toy car.

standard: Open Tools → “Speed of light” and choose the “Signal delay” tab.
Pick a world, or click one in the scene.
simple: Press Tools, then “How fast is light?”.
Click “Signal delay” and pick Mars.

what.standard: How long light takes from the nearest star, the centre of our galaxy and the Andromeda galaxy.
what.simple: Light from far stars is very, very old when it gets here.

why.standard: When you look at a star you see the past: Andromeda’s light set off long before the first modern humans lived.
why.simple: Looking at stars is like looking back in time!

standard: Open Tools → “Speed of light” and choose the “Farther out” tab.
simple: Press Tools, then “How fast is light?”.
Click “Farther out”.

what.standard: Two or more worlds next to each other at their true relative sizes, with plain comparisons: how many fit inside, what you would weigh, how long their days and years are.
what.simple: See two worlds next to each other at their real sizes.

why.standard: Earth next to the Sun is a dot you have to look for: sizes finally make sense when they share one picture.
why.simple: Next to the Sun, Earth is a tiny dot!

standard: On a world’s card, press “Compare with…”, or open Tools → “Side by side”.
Change either world with the pickers, add more with “Add…”, or click one in the row to compare it instead.
The camera button makes a picture of the comparison.
simple: On a planet’s card, press “Compare with…”.
Pick another world to compare.

what.standard: Fifteen ready-made comparisons in three groups, Sizes, Moons and Surprises, each opening with the one fact that makes its point: “Earth’s twin”, “Moons bigger than a planet”, “Where would you weigh the most?”.
what.simple: Pick a ready-made comparison, like all eight planets in a row.

why.standard: Each one starts a class discussion in one click: the link above opens the moons that are bigger than the planet Mercury.
why.simple: Did you know some moons are bigger than a planet?

standard: On the comparison page, open Ideas.
Pick one; its name appears above the facts. Click any world in the row to talk about it.
simple: Press Ideas.
Pick “All eight planets”.

what.standard: Narrated step-by-step tours: the app moves the camera and sets the date, speed and scale, while a card says what you are looking at. Four are ready: the Grand Tour, how big space really is, how we know the Earth moves, and where there could be life.
what.simple: Let the app show you around, stop by stop, while a card tells you what you see.

why.standard: A tour turns the sandbox into a ready-made lesson, and the class can still look around at any stop: the tour waits.
why.simple: You do not have to know where to go. And you can look around at every stop!

standard: Press “Tours” at the bottom right and pick a tour.
Step with “Next” and “Back” on the card, the arrow keys, or a presenter remote (Page Down / Page Up).

Look around at any time; “Back to the tour” restores the stop. “Autoplay” moves on by itself, and the link button copies a link to the current stop. Teachers can write their own tours as data (src/data/tours/README.md).
simple: Press “Tours” at the bottom right and pick one.
Read the card, then press “Next” or an arrow key.
Look around whenever you like, then press “Back to the tour”.

present.title: Projector mode
present.what: Larger text, names and buttons, readable from the back of the room.
present.why: A laptop screen on a projector is too small to read; projector mode fixes that with one key.
how: Open Present at the top right and choose “Large text for a projector”, or press P.
Everything else keeps working: keys, links and the controls.

contrast.title: High contrast
contrast.what: Stronger colours and outlines for washed-out projectors and bright rooms.
contrast.why: A pale beamer in daylight hides grey text and faint lines; high contrast keeps everything legible.
how: Open Present and choose “High contrast”, or press C.
It also switches on by itself when the computer asks for more contrast.

presenterKeys.title: Keyboard and presenter remote
presenterKeys.what: Every step of a lesson has a key, and a presenter remote’s buttons step from planet to planet.
presenterKeys.why: Stay at the front of the room: 1 to 8 fly to the planets, 0 shows the whole system, S changes the scale, L hides the names.
how: Page Down and Page Up (the remote’s buttons) go to the next or previous world, or step through a tour.
The table of controls below lists them all.

hideControls.title: Hide the controls
hideControls.what: Take every button and panel off the screen, so only space is left.
hideControls.why: For looking, for screenshots and for a projector: the class sees the solar system, not the interface.
how: Press H, or the crossed-out eye at the top right (it is also in the Present menu). It works with or without presenting.
Press H again, or move the mouse and click “Show the controls”, to bring them back. Keys keep working while hidden.

prepareLesson.title: Prepare a lesson
prepareLesson.what: The address of the page is the lesson: it holds the world, camera, date, speed, scale, layers, language and whether time is paused.
prepareLesson.why: Set up a view before class, bookmark it, and it opens exactly the same in front of the students.
how: Set up the view, pause time if you want it to open still, and bookmark the page or copy its address.
In class, open the link; press R (or Home) at any time to go back to exactly that start.
Press Esc to leave to the whole system.

share.title: Share with the class
share.what: A link to exactly what is on screen, with a copy button and a QR code big enough to scan from the back row.
share.why: Students open the same view on their own tablets and explore from there, with no typing.
how: Open Share at the top right.
Copy the link, or press “Show the QR code to the class”.

ownHunt.title: Make your own scavenger hunt
ownHunt.what: Pick clues from the whole question bank and turn them into a hunt for your lesson.
ownHunt.why: The hunt fits the topic of the day, and a link starts it for every student in your language.
how: Open Tools → “Scavenger hunt” and choose “Make your own hunt”.
Tick the clues, then Start, or Share to get the link for the class.

what.standard: Clues to solve by finding the right world in the scene and clicking it, with hints when you are stuck and a story when you find it.
what.simple: Read a clue, find the right world, and click it!

why.standard: Searching makes you explore: there is no score and no timer, and every wrong guess is a world you just visited.
why.simple: You learn a lot while you look. There is no timer, and no losing.

standard: Open Tools at the bottom right, choose “Scavenger hunt” and pick a hunt: Easy, Medium or Tricky.
Read the clue, find the world and click it.
Stuck? “Need a hint?”, and after the last hint “Show me”.
simple: Press Tools, then “Scavenger hunt”.
Pick an easy hunt.
Read the clue and click the right world.

title.simple: How old are you on Mars?

what.standard: Pick your birth date to see your age on every planet, your next birthday there, the days you have lived and how far Earth has carried you around the Sun.
what.simple: Find out how old you are on other planets, and when your next birthday there is.

why.standard: A year is one lap around the Sun, so on Mars you are about half your age and on Mercury four times older.
why.simple: A year on Mars is almost two Earth years, so you are younger there!

standard: Open Tools at the bottom right, choose “Your birthday” and pick the year, the month and the day.
The planets fly to the day you were born; ⏭ next to a planet travels to your next birthday there.
Your date is never saved or sent anywhere: it is forgotten when you close the page, or at once with “Forget my birthday”.
simple: Press Tools, then “Your birthday”.
Pick your year, month and day.
Read how old you are on each planet.

what.standard: Turn what is on screen into a postcard with the date, a caption, an honest note about the scale and a QR code back to the view.
what.simple: Make a picture of what you see, to save or send.

why.standard: Something to keep, print or send home, and the QR code opens the same view again.
why.simple: Keep your favourite view of space, or show it at home.

standard: Open Tools at the bottom right and choose “Take a picture”.
Write a caption, switch the names or the QR code off.
Save, copy or share the picture. It is made on your device; nothing is uploaded.
simple: Press Tools at the bottom right, then “Take a picture”.
Write something about your picture.
Press Save picture.

what.standard: A short form that sends your bug report, idea or question straight to the people who make Orbitalia, with the view you were looking at attached if you like.
what.simple: Write to the people who make Orbitalia when something is broken or when you have an idea.

why.standard: Orbitalia is open source and grows with what teachers, students and space fans tell us; a link to the broken view makes a bug quick to fix.
why.simple: Your idea could be in the app next time!

standard: On the solar system, open the arrow next to Help at the top right and choose “Send feedback”: the view you are looking at goes with it, if you like.
Choose what it is about, write a few words and press “Send”. Your email is optional: give it only if you would like an answer.
With a GitHub account you can also report it on GitHub or talk with others in GitHub Discussions; the page links to both.
simple: Press the arrow next to Help, then “Tell us what you think”.
Write what is broken, or your idea.
Press “Send”. You do not need to give your email.

turn.action: Turn around the world you are looking at

zoom.mouse: Mouse wheel, trackpad pinch, or drag with the middle button

move.mouse: Drag with the right button, or Shift + drag

back.action: Back to the whole solar system
back.mouse: Click the house button at the top left
back.touch: Tap the house button at the top left

hint.action: See what a switch or button does

siblings.action: Next or previous world of the same family

planets.action: The planets from Mercury (1) to Neptune (8), the whole system (0)

speed.mouse: The speed button next to the date
speed.touch: The speed button next to the date

start.action: Back to the view the link opened with

scale.action: Next scale: Everything visible, Textbook, True scale

sound.action: Sound on or off (always off when the app opens)

data.title: Data
data.intro: Where the numbers come from: sizes, orbits, rotation and dates.

maps.title: Surface maps
maps.intro: The pictures wrapped around the globes.

sounds.title: Sounds
sounds.intro: The recordings you can listen to. The app’s own tones are made in the browser.

software.title: Software
software.intro: Open-source building blocks the app is made from.

app.title: This app
app.intro: Orbitalia is open source: anyone may use it, study it, improve it and share it.

credits.solarSystemApi: The starting list of the Sun, planets and moons: sizes, masses, orbits and discovery details.
credits.jpl: Accurate orbits for the planets, the Moon, the Galilean moons and Phoebe (mean orbital elements), used to correct the list.
credits.iau: Where every pole points and how fast each world turns, so the Sun is overhead at Greenwich at noon.
credits.meeus: How the Moon’s orbit slowly turns, so eclipses land on their real dates.
credits.rings: The rings of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, drawn for this app from published ring radii, opacities and colours.
credits.spaceAudio: Four real recordings of radio and plasma waves, measured by Cassini, Voyager 1 and Injun 3 and turned into sound.
credits.three: Draws the 3D scene in the browser.
credits.tanstack: Pages and the links that hold every view.
credits.gsap: Page transitions and the dictionary’s animations.
credits.smallLibraries: App state, data checks, dates, QR codes and translations with plurals.
credits.orbitalia: Made by the Orbitalia contributors. Anyone can add a feature, a tour or a translation.

licences.openData: published as open data (no formal licence named)
licences.noKnownRestrictions: no known restrictions (check before commercial use)
